title: Tokenization serviceization: cost, reliability and perf probe
content:
Summary:

This doc captures an experiment series to evaluate moving tokenization out of the main request worker process into a separate tokenization microservice (same-host vs remote) and alternative interop strategies (UDS, shared-mmap, inproc cooperative thread). The goal is to understand the tradeoffs on short-tail CPU cost, tail latency, and operational reliability for small request workloads (single-turn prompts, <128 tokens) which dominate our hosted traffic.

Motivation / background:
- We continue to see CPU tail spikes on small requests even when model paths are optimized. Profiling indicates a non-trivial fraction of that time (~20-35%) is spent in request preproc: header parsing, JSON deserialization, and tokenization (UTF8 scan + vocab lookup).
- Tokenization is attractive to surface as an isolated service because it is stateless and can be specialized (SIMD-optimized scanning, smaller working set). But network/IPC overhead can erase benefit for microsecond-scale operations.

Hypotheses:
1) Offloading tokenization to a same-host UDS microservice will reduce GIL contention in Python worker and lower p95 for multi-request bursts by avoiding blocking Python-level tokenizer code.
2) Serialization overhead (msgpack/CBOR) will add fixed latency; using shared-memory (mmap + ringbuffer) reduces that overhead but increases implementation complexity and risk.
3) For very small requests (<32 tokens), in-process optimized tokenizer with cooperative yielding (pyshim/park-unpark) will still be lowest latency; serviceization helps most when CPU saturation causes contention across requests.

Experiment design:
- Workloads: three synthetic mixes derived from production traces (sanitized):
  * micro: 1–16 token responses, median request body 300B, 70% of traffic
  * small: 16–64 tokens, median 1.1KB
  * medium: 64–256 tokens, larger payloads
- Baselines: current in-process Python tokenizer (baseline v0).
- Variants:
  A) UDS JSON-over-HTTP-lite microservice (same host) using uvicorn + fastapi, msgpack body
  B) UDS raw framed msgpack binary to Rust tokenizer process (tokio, SIMD UTF8 scan)
  C) Shared-memory ringbuffer + synchronization (mmap + futex) to Rust tokenizer process (same host)
  D) Inproc cooperative threadpool tokenizer using a Rust extension (pybind) pinned to separate cores (pyshim park/unpark approach)
  E) Remote tokenizer over loopback-like latency (simulate 0.5ms added one-way)

- Metrics collected:
  * p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency
  * pure tokenization CPU time (measured with perf and ratelimiting via cgroups)
  * worker-side blocked time (GIL wait, syscalls) via py-spy and pyinstrument
  * throughput under load (reqs/s) until 95th percentile latency crosses SLO (100ms)
  * additional cost proxy: extra CPU cycles per request and estimated $/1M requests
- Tools: perf, py-spy, eBPF (bcc tracepoints), flamegraphs (FlameScope), strace sampling for syscall hotspots.

Key microbench harness notes:
- Each experiment run: 5m warmup, 10m measurement, concurrent client streams to simulate 200–1000 rps depending on workload.
- CPU isolation: worker pinned to 8 vCPU, tokenizer variants pinned to separate cores when appropriate to measure cross-saturation.
- Serialization formats compared: JSON, msgpack, custom binary framing.

Results (summary of median run across 3 repeats):
- Baseline (inproc Python tokenizer): micro p50=3.6ms p95=12.8ms p99=28.1ms; tokenization contribution median 1.1ms, p95 6.0ms. Significant time in Python UTF8 scanning + dict lookups (vocab).
- Variant A (UDS HTTP/msgpack, Python tokenizer service): micro p50=5.1ms p95=15.9ms p99=34.5ms. Plain UDS+HTTP cost ~1.2ms median added; serialization + context switch dominates. No reduction in tokenization CPU because same Python code.
- Variant B (UDS framed msgpack to Rust SIMD tokenizer): micro p50=3.0ms p95=9.4ms p99=22.7ms. Tokenization CPU dropped by ~55% median; p95 improved by ~26% vs baseline. UDS roundtrip ~0.35ms median.
- Variant C (shared-mmap ringbuffer to Rust): micro p50=2.7ms p95=8.5ms p99=20.2ms. Serialization cost essentially eliminated; however engineering complexity and occasional stall observed due to futex wakeup spikes under extreme contention.
- Variant D (inproc Rust extension pinned core): micro p50=2.6ms p95=7.9ms p99=19.8ms. Lowest absolute latency in most cases because no IPC and no Python-level UTF8 scan. However this requires native extension management and careful GIL release semantics.
- Variant E (remote): adds ~0.7–1.5ms consistent overhead; remote service only wins when Rust tokenizer cuts tokenization CPU by >3x and system is CPU saturated.

Observations / flamegraph notes:
- Baseline: Python UTF8 decode loop and repeated .get() on Python dict (vocab) dominate tokenization time. Garbage from small temporary string allocations visible.
- UDS+HTTP: context switches and uvicorn worker handshake visible; socket send/recv syscalls account for most of added overhead.
- Framed binary to Rust: clear shift of CPU from Python user-space into a few hot Rust functions (utf8_scan_simd, byte_to_id_lookup). System calls minimal.
- Shared-mmap: kernel futex/unmap churn visible at high concurrency; serialization cost negligible.
- Inproc Rust extension: major benefit is elimination of both Python allocation churn and IPC. But we observed two risks: (1) safety in multi-tenant process if tokenizer bug causes process crash, (2) harder to evolve tokenizer C ABI.

Cost estimates (back-of-envelope):
- Baseline tokenization CPU cycle cost ~ 0.9k cycles/request extra on small requests = ~0.25 vCPU-s / 1M requests.
- UDS overhead adds ~0.35 vCPU-s / 1M requests for same-host HTTP+uvicorn; UDS framed binary ~0.09 vCPU-s / 1M requests.
- Running a dedicated tokenizer pool (Rust) on shared hosts estimated cost parity when tokenizer reduces model-side CPU by >15% under heavy load. For our current traffic mix the break-even is ~300k req/day per tokenizer worker core.

Reliability and operational notes:
- Introducing a separate tokenizer service increases blast radius (availability dependency). Must add healthchecking, local fallback to inproc tokenizer, circuit breaker and slow-start backoff.
- Shared-mmap approach complicates autoscaling across nodes; harder to debug and requires consistent kernel ABI tuning. We saw sporadic futex stalls with >128 concurrent clients in the same host.
- Inproc Rust extension increases single-process risk but simplifies routing and avoids IPC complexity. Requires extra QA (fuzzing, ASAN/UBSAN builds) and stronger CI gating.

Short-term recommendations (what we can try in next 2–4 weeks):
1) Prototype Variant B (UDS framed binary to Rust tokenizer) behind a feature flag for Dedicated deployments only. This has clear perf wins while keeping isolation via process boundary.
2) Implement worker-side circuit breaker + fallback to inproc tokenizer when tokenizer svc p50>10ms or connection errors >1%.
3) Add a lightweight msgpack binary framing benchmark harness to our perf repo and a monitoring dashboard for tokenizer latencies.
4) Instrument production sampling to capture tokenization timings at request-level (non-blocking via async traces) so we can validate improvements on live traffic.

Medium-term (1–3 months):
1) Evaluate inproc Rust extension (Variant D) as an opt-in build for high-perf Dedicated images where customer wants the lowest latency and accepts single-process risk.
2) If we pursue shared-mmap (Variant C), prototype a robust futex backoff policy and a cross-language ringbuffer library with versioning to reduce maintenance cost.
3) Explore vocabulary cache optimization: compact C-level trie for id lookup instead of Python dict to reduce allocations and branch mispredicts. This could give many benefits without serviceization.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- What is acceptable blast radius for a tokenizer outage? Do we want default fallback to slower inproc or fail closed?
- Can we open a small oncall playbook for tokenizer process restarts and automated fallback?
- How much risk tolerance for adding native extensions in hosted environments? (legal/third-party binary concerns?)

Appendix: commands and notes:
- perf recording: perf record -F 99 -g --pid <pid> -o perf.data -- sleep 60
- py-spy top: py-spy top --pid <pid> --nonblocking --rate 20 --duration 60
- eBPF small script used to measure futex vs sendmsg rates (attached to PR 987)
- harness command for framed UDS run: ./harness --clients 400 --uds /var/run/tokenizer.sock --format framed-msgpack --duration 600

Owners and next steps:
- Owner: Aisha Patel (implement prototype B, test harness integration)
- Action: Marco to draft fallback circuit-breaker implementation; Priya to add tokenizer latency charts to console prototype; Evan to run extended stress runs and share flamegraphs.

Notes to reviewers: this is an exploratory doc. Numbers are median from lab runs on c6i-like instances (8 vCPU) with synthetic traffic modelled from scrubbed production traces. Expect some variance in cloud instances with different kernel versions and NIC offloads.
